analysis.one_liner: Ends the exemption that denies farmworkers overtime pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Farmworkers are the largest group of workers still excluded from overtime pay under federal law. This bill would have required farm employers to pay time-and-a-half after 55 hours a week starting in 2021, stepping down to 40 hours by 2024, with small farms (25 or fewer employees) getting extra years to comply. It also repealed other agriculture-related exemptions, including for sugar processing, cotton ginning, and small farms. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers — a workforce that is heavily immigrant and among the lowest-paid in the country — would gain overtime pay for hours beyond a weekly threshold that starts at 55 and falls to 40. Workers at sugar processing, cotton ginning, and irrigation operations would gain the same overtime rights other workers already have. Small farms would benefit from a longer phase-in.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in 2021, farm employers would owe one-and-a-half times the regular rate for hours beyond 55 a week, with the threshold falling to 50, 45, and then 40 hours by 2024 [S2] [S3].
Employers with 25 or fewer employees would not have to start paying overtime until 2024, with the threshold reaching 40 hours only in 2027 [S2] [S3].

The bill repeals the overtime exemption for agriculture-related employers such as small farms, irrigation projects, sugar processing, and cotton ginning and compressing, closing a carve-out that dates to the original 1938 law [S2] [S3].
The overtime requirement would not apply to immediate family members of the employer, as under current law [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farm employers — growers, sugar processors, cotton ginners, and irrigation operators — would bear the cost of overtime wages, and some of that cost would likely show up in food prices or in reduced hours. Small farms get a phase-in but face the same requirement eventually.

drawbacks.text: Overtime costs fall on farm employers, including small farms, which face the same requirements as large operations after the phase-in ends — the bill gives smaller employers later start dates (2024-2027) rather than a permanent exemption [S2] [S3].

A good-faith objection is that agriculture operates on harvest-driven schedules where weeks over 55 hours are common and seasonal; a hard weekly overtime threshold could lead growers to cap hours, cutting workers' total earnings in peak weeks even as their hourly rate rises after the threshold.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: one of the lowest-paid workforces in the country would gain a protection — overtime pay — that nearly every other hourly worker has had since 1938. The cost is real for farm employers, especially small ones, which is why the bill built in long phase-ins and a higher initial threshold. The most honest concern is that a weekly hour trigger in seasonal work can backfire by capping hours; a version designed around that reality might serve workers better.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the Fairness for Farm Workers Act on February 7, 2019, with 18 original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day, and no further action appears in its record [S5].
66 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from one party [S4].
The House and Senate never voted on the bill, and it expired at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm employers are better off because the bill died: they keep paying no overtime for hours beyond 40 a week, a carve-out from the Fair Labor Standards Act that has existed since 1938. Farmworkers remain the largest excluded group.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm employers who pay no overtime

sides.party_line_note: All 66 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the record shows no Republican action on the bill at any stage [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Growers would have owed time-and-a-half for hours beyond a weekly threshold, a payroll cost they avoid under the 1938 exemption. Ordinary farmworkers would have been the direct beneficiaries, so the industry's interest ran against theirs.
The bill gave small employers a delayed phase-in starting in 2024 and not reaching 40 hours until 2027, easing the burden while still eventually extending overtime rights to their workers.

industries.industry: Sugar processing, cotton ginning, and irrigation operators
industries.note: The bill repealed their specific overtime exemptions, exposing these agriculture-related employers to the same overtime rules as other industries.
